title: SIP core: messages, transactions, dialogs
summary: Roles, methods, headers, transaction timers, dialog identity, and the transports those rules sit on.

lessons.title: Roles a trace is actually showing
lessons.summary: A trace shows a user agent, a proxy, a registrar, a redirect server, or a B2BUA, and products often combine those roles.
objectives: Separate UAC and UAS from the box name
Predict what a redirect server leaves behind
Recognize a B2BUA by the second dialog

illustration.title: Who speaks SIP
illustration.caption: The location service is a database the proxy consults. It is not a request method.

layers.name: UAC / UAS
layers.detail: Builds the request or the response

layers.name: B2BUA
layers.detail: Two dialogs joined by the application

sections.h: The same box changes roles per request
paragraphs: The UAC is the role that creates a request. The UAS is the role that creates the response. A phone is a UAC for the INVITE it sends and a UAS for the INVITE it answers.

A stateful proxy maintains the transaction, adds a Via with its own branch, and decrements Max-Forwards. A stateless proxy forwards without that transaction state and does not generate its own 100 Trying. A redirect server returns 3xx with a Contact and does not stay in the dialog.

The registrar accepts REGISTER and writes bindings into a location service. The proxy reads that location service when it retargets. RFC 3261 keeps those roles separate even when one product runs both.

A B2BUA is a UAS glued to a UAC. It usually creates a new Call-ID on the outgoing side. RFC 7092 classifies that behavior, and RFC 5853 describes SBC requirements. If the Call-ID changes in the middle of the ladder, you are not looking at a pure proxy.

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: The redirect server is the UAS for this transaction only.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKred1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: 302 gives a Contact and creates no ongoing dialog to stay in.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 302 Moved Temporarily
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKred1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=red9
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:+15551212@203.0.113.20>
Content-Length: 0

steps.label: ACK
steps.note: The non-2xx ACK uses the INVITE branch. The redirect server is done.
steps.message:
ACK sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKred1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=red9
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 ACK
Content-Length: 0

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: A new transaction, new branch, new Call-ID, aimed at the Contact.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@203.0.113.20 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKprox1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: b7c8d9e0f1@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: The proxy generates 100. It will not relay a downstream 100.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 100 Trying
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKprox1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: b7c8d9e0f1@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: Proxy Via on top, Max-Forwards 69, Contact left as the caller's.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.20;branch=z9hG4bKprox2
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKprox1
Max-Forwards: 69
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: b7c8d9e0f1@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: The peer is the UAS. Its Contact becomes the remote target.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.20;branch=z9hG4bKprox2
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKprox1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: b7c8d9e0f1@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40>
Content-Length: 197

o=peer 10 11 IN IP4 192.0.2.40

choices: The role that creates the request
Always the phone on the right
quiz.why: The same device is a UAS when it answers.
The Contact in the 3xx is the next Request-URI. The redirect server does not proxy the call.

choices: Keeps transaction state and can generate 100 Trying
quiz.why: A stateless proxy does not hold that state and does not generate 100.

quiz.q: Registrar and proxy in RFC 3261 are
choices: Separate roles that products often combine
Two names for the same transaction
quiz.why: REGISTER writes bindings. The proxy consults a location service.

quiz.q: A strong sign of a B2BUA is
choices: A new Call-ID on the outgoing leg
quiz.why: A pure proxy preserves Call-ID. RFC 7092 describes the B2BUA.

choices: Is the store of bindings a proxy consults
quiz.why: It is logical state. REGISTER is how a UA writes it.

cards.back: Creates a request. Defined with the rest of the user-agent rules.
Transaction state, own Via branch, own 100 Trying.
3xx and a Contact, then it is out of the call.

lab.title: Who is still on the ladder?
lab.prompt: After the ACK of the 302, which role is finished?
steps: Step through the 302 and its ACK.
Name the role that does not appear again.

check.q: After the ACK of the 302, the redirect server
choices: Is finished and is not on the second call
check.why: A redirect server does not proxy the follow-up INVITE.

fault.title: Proxy that changed Call-ID
fault.symptom: The ladder is documented as a pure proxy, but the outgoing INVITE has a different Call-ID and a different From tag.
fault.log:
IN: Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com From tag=9fxced76sl
OUT: Call-ID: b7c8d9e0f1@example.com From tag=edge99
Via count increased, Max-Forwards decreased
choices: This leg is a B2BUA, not a pure proxy
Call-ID must change at every proxy
Max-Forwards caused a new dialog id
fault.why: A proxy preserves Call-ID, From tag, and To tag. A new Call-ID means a new dialog created by a UAC inside a B2BUA.
fault.cause: The box terminated the incoming dialog and originated another.
fault.fix: Trace both Call-IDs as two dialogs. Cite RFC 7092 if the design claimed this hop was a proxy.

lessons.title: Methods and status codes
lessons.summary: The core methods are INVITE, ACK, OPTIONS, BYE, CANCEL, and REGISTER, and status codes fall into six classes.
objectives: Place a code in the 1xx through 6xx classes
Match ACK and CANCEL to the INVITE they belong to
Separate 401 from 407

illustration.title: Classes you will say out loud
illustration.caption: The reason phrase is a hint. The code is the rule.
rows: This sender can often fix it

paragraphs: RFC 3261 defines INVITE, ACK, OPTIONS, BYE, CANCEL, and REGISTER. INVITE sets up a session. ACK finishes the INVITE handshake. BYE ends a confirmed dialog. CANCEL asks to abandon an INVITE that has no final response yet.
OPTIONS asks for capabilities and does not set up a session. REGISTER writes bindings. PRACK, UPDATE, and REFER are extension methods: RFC 3262, RFC 3311, and RFC 3515. They do not replace the six.
100 Trying is hop by hop. 180 means ringing. 183 means session progress and often carries early media SDP. 200 OK is success. 302 moves you to a Contact.

401 Unauthorized challenges a UAS or registrar with WWW-Authenticate. 407 Proxy Authentication Required challenges a proxy. 486 is Busy Here. 487 is Request Terminated, the usual final response after a successful CANCEL. 603 Decline is a global rejection. Section 22 is the authentication chapter.

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: INVITE is the session request. CSeq method token is INVITE.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKbusy1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: 100 is provisional. The transaction is still open.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 100 Trying
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKbusy1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: 180 is also provisional. A To tag creates an early dialog.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 180 Ringing
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKbusy1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40>
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: 486 Busy Here is a final 4xx. The early dialog does not become confirmed.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 486 Busy Here
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKbusy1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

steps.label: ACK
steps.note: The ACK for a non-2xx reuses the INVITE branch. CSeq is 1 ACK.
steps.message:
ACK sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKbusy1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 ACK
Content-Length: 0

choices: An INVITE that has no final response yet
quiz.why: BYE is the method that ends a confirmed dialog.
The call will not proceed on this response. ACK it inside the INVITE transaction.

choices: 401 challenges the UAS or registrar, 407 challenges a proxy
quiz.why: WWW-Authenticate versus Proxy-Authenticate. Section 22.
Section 11. A 200 OK may include Allow.

quiz.q: 487 Request Terminated is the usual final response
quiz.why: The CANCEL itself gets 200 OK. The INVITE gets 487, then a non-2xx ACK.
A forking proxy treats 6xx as a reason to stop other branches.

cards.back: Set up, complete the handshake, and end a confirmed dialog.
Abandon an unanswered INVITE. It is not BYE.
UAS or registrar challenge versus proxy challenge.
Provisional. The transaction is still waiting for a final response.

lab.title: Class the code
lab.prompt: Dissect the final response in this lab message, which is the 486.
lab.message:
SIP/2.0 486 Busy Here
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKbusy1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

check.why: Busy Here is local to this UAS. 603 would be the global form.

fault.title: BYE used to cancel a setup
fault.symptom: The caller hears ringing and the trace shows BYE with no To tag, then 481.
fault.log:
BYE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKbye1
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 2 BYE
Content-Length: 0

SIP/2.0 481 Call/Transaction Does Not Exist
choices: BYE needs an established dialog. CANCEL is the method while INVITE is unanswered
fault.why: There is no confirmed dialog to end. The INVITE is still outstanding, so CANCEL matches that transaction.
fault.cause: BYE was sent with no To tag, outside a dialog.
fault.fix: Send CANCEL with the INVITE's branch and CSeq number, then ACK the 487.

lessons.title: Headers and compact forms
lessons.summary: Compact header names are aliases from RFC 3261, with a few more aliases defined in the extension RFCs.
objectives: Expand the RFC 3261 compact forms
Keep extension compact forms with their RFCs
See why rewriting From or To breaks dialog matching

illustration.title: Compact names
illustration.caption: One character is the whole header name. Unknown one-letter names are not a license to invent aliases.

sections.h: Long form and short form are one header
paragraphs: A header is a name, a colon, and a value. RFC 3261 defines compact forms for ten headers: c Content-Type, e Content-Encoding, f From, i Call-ID, k Supported, l Content-Length, m Contact, s Subject, t To, and v Via.

The compact form is only a size alias. f is From, including the tag. A parser that stores the long name and a parser that stores the short name are talking about the same field. Section 7.3.3 and section 20 are the citations.
Event's compact form is o, and Allow-Events is u. Those two come from RFC 6665, not from the base list. Refer-To is r and Referred-By is b, from RFC 3515.

Rewriting From, To, or Call-ID is not a compact-form conversion. Those fields are the dialog identity. A SIP profile that substitutes a different URI into From will make the peer's later requests fail to match the dialog.

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: v, f, t, i, m, and l are the compact names. The branch cookie is still required.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
v: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKcmp1
Max-Forwards: 70
f: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
t: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
i: compact-1@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
m: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
l: 0
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: The response uses the long names. It matches on the branch, not on the spelling of Via.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 100 Trying
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKcmp1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: To now has a tag. The compact t on the request was the same To header.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKcmp1
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40>
Content-Length: 0

steps.label: ACK
steps.note: The ACK is written in long form. CSeq is 1 ACK.
steps.message:
ACK sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKcmpAck
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 ACK
Content-Length: 0

quiz.q: The compact form of Call-ID is
quiz.why: c is Content-Type. o is Event, from RFC 6665.

quiz.q: The compact form of Contact is
quiz.why: m is Contact. c is Content-Type.

quiz.q: Event's compact form o is defined in
quiz.why: Do not add o to the base list of ten.
b is Referred-By, also RFC 3515. t is To.

choices: Only the header name on the wire
quiz.why: f and From are the same header. The tag inside the value still identifies the dialog.

quiz.q: A profile that replaces the From URI
choices: Can prevent the peer from matching the dialog
quiz.why: From tag and From URI are dialog state. Compact form does not ask you to edit them.

cards.back: Via, From, To, Call-ID.
Contact, Content-Length, Content-Type, Supported.
Event and Allow-Events. RFC 6665.
Refer-To and Referred-By. RFC 3515.

lab.title: Rewrite From on purpose
lab.prompt: Run the profile. It is legal syntax and a dangerous edit. See which URI the From header contains afterward.
steps: Compare the From URI with the original.
lab.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@203.0.113.20 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bK7766as01
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Supported: 100rel,replaces,timer
Allow: INVITE,ACK,CANCEL,BYE,UPDATE,PRACK,OPTIONS,REFER
Content-Length: 0

check.q: The profile replaces alice@example.com inside From with
check.why: The teaching profile substitutes the user. The dialog id still depends on the original From.

fault.title: 481 after a From rewrite
fault.symptom: The SBC rewrites the From URI on the INVITE. The callee answers, and the caller's ACK gets 481.
fault.log:
request INVITE sip-header From modify "alice@example.com" "+15551212@example.com"
ACK sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40 SIP/2.0
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
SIP/2.0 481 Call/Transaction Does Not Exist
choices: The dialog was created with a different From URI than the ACK presents
fault.why: The peer stored the From it was given. The ACK still has the caller's original From.
fault.cause: A SIP profile changed From on one hop only.
fault.fix: Stop rewriting From and To. If a number must change, change the Request-URI or a diversion identity and leave the dialog tags intact.

lessons.title: Transactions and the branch cookie
lessons.summary: A transaction is identified by the branch, and a retransmission repeats that branch instead of starting a new one.
objectives: Use the branch as the transaction id
Separate a retransmission from a new request
Apply the ACK branch rule for 2xx and non-2xx

illustration.title: INVITE client transaction
illustration.caption: Calling retransmits. Proceeding waits. A 2xx is handed to the transaction user because its ACK is a new transaction.

paragraphs: The branch parameter identifies the transaction. An implementation of RFC 3261 starts it with z9hG4bK and makes the rest unique across space and time. A retransmission sends the same request again, including that branch.

CANCEL is an exception: it uses the same branch as the INVITE it cancels. The ACK for a non-2xx final response uses that same branch too. The ACK for a 2xx does not. It is a different transaction, so it gets a new branch.

sections.h: INVITE is the special state machine
paragraphs: On UDP the client starts in Calling, retransmits at T1 doubling, and starts Timer B at 64 times T1. A provisional response moves it to Proceeding and stops those retransmissions. If Timer B fires, the client must not invent an ACK.

The overview in section 17 calls INVITE a three-way handshake. RFC 6026 corrects the 2xx path: the transaction user sends the end-to-end ACK, and the transaction layer absorbs late 2xx responses. The non-2xx ACK is still generated hop by hop inside the INVITE transaction.

flow.title: Retransmit, then a new ACK branch

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: Calling state. Timer A starts at T1 on UDP. Branch z9hG4bKtx01.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKtx01
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Content-Length: 0

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: Timer A fired. Same branch, so this is the same transaction, not a new call.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKtx01
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@203.0.113.10>
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: Proceeding. Retransmissions of the INVITE stop. Still no To tag on this 100.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 100 Trying
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKtx01
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: Final 2xx. The Via branch still names the INVITE transaction.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKtx01
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40>
Content-Length: 197

v=0
o=peer 10 11 IN IP4 192.0.2.40
s=-
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.40
t=0 0
m=audio 19642 RTP/AVP 0 101
a=rtpmap:0 PCMU/8000
a=rtpmap:101 telephone-event/8000
a=fmtp:101 0-16
a=ptime:20
a=sendrecv

steps.label: ACK
steps.note: New branch z9hG4bKtxAck. CSeq number stays 1 and the method token is ACK.
steps.message:
ACK sip:+15551212@192.0.2.40 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/UDP 203.0.113.10;branch=z9hG4bKtxAck
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=9fxced76sl
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=314159
Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com
CSeq: 1 ACK
Content-Length: 0

choices: The same branch on the same request
quiz.why: The transaction id does not change when Timer A fires.
It is its own transaction. The CSeq number still matches the INVITE.

choices: Is end to end through every proxy as a new transaction
quiz.why: Non-2xx ACK stays inside the INVITE transaction and is hop by hop.

quiz.q: If Timer B fires, the INVITE client
quiz.why: There is no final response to acknowledge. The transaction user learns about the timeout.
The 2xx ACK stays end to end. The transaction layer's job is to absorb the late responses.

choices: The same value as the INVITE it cancels
quiz.why: That is how the server transaction finds the INVITE to abandon.

cards.back: Transaction identifier. Cookie z9hG4bK plus a unique token.
Same message, same branch, sent again by the transaction timer.
New transaction, new branch, end to end. CSeq number matches the INVITE.

lessons.title: Dialog identity
lessons.summary: A dialog is identified by Call-ID, the From tag, and the To tag, and the initial request has no To tag.
objectives: Name the three dialog-id components
Tell an early dialog from a confirmed dialog
Increment CSeq for a new request inside the dialog

illustration.title: Dialog states
illustration.caption: No dialog exists until a response carries a To tag. BYE moves a confirmed dialog to terminated.

paragraphs: Dialog identity is the Call-ID, the From tag, and the To tag. At the UAC the local tag is the From tag and the remote tag is the To tag. At the UAS the local and remote tags are swapped, and the three values are the same set.

A request outside a dialog has no To tag. The UAS puts the tag on the response that creates the dialog. A 100 Trying SHOULD NOT add that tag. A 180 or 183 that includes a tag creates an early dialog. A 2xx to the INVITE confirms it.

The remote target is the Contact URI from the other side. Later requests in the dialog use that URI as the Request-URI, and they carry both tags. The route set, if Record-Route was present, is stored with the dialog.

The CSeq number increases for each new request the UAC sends inside the dialog. ACK and CANCEL are the exceptions that keep the INVITE's number and change only the method token. BYE is a new request, so its CSeq number is higher, and it is how a confirmed dialog ends.

lessons.title: T1, the transaction timeout, and Timer C
lessons.summary: T1 seeds retransmissions, 64 times T1 ends the transaction, and Timer C is the proxy's longer INVITE arm.
objectives: State the defaults for T1, T2, and T4
Compute Timer B as 64 times T1
Keep Timer C separate from Timer B

illustration.title: Clocks from the timer table
illustration.caption: Change T1 and every timer that scales with it changes. Timer C does not use that formula.
rows: Timer B and Timer F give-up
Proxy wait for a final INVITE response
Retransmit cap, and time left in the network

paragraphs: T1 is an estimate of the round trip and defaults to 500 ms. On UDP, Timer A starts at T1 and doubles after each INVITE retransmission while the client is in Calling. A reliable transport does not start Timer A.

T2 defaults to 4 seconds and caps the spacing of non-INVITE retransmissions and of INVITE response retransmissions. T4 defaults to 5 seconds and is the time a message may still be in the network. Timer I and Timer K use T4 on UDP so a stray retransmission can be absorbed.

Timer B is the INVITE transaction timeout and Timer F is the non-INVITE transaction timeout. Both are 64 times T1, which is 32 seconds at the default. Seven UDP transmissions fit in that window. If Timer B fires, the client does not generate an ACK.

Timer C belongs to the proxy, not to that formula. It is how long a proxy will wait for a final response to INVITE, and the table sets it at more than 3 minutes. A proxy that abandons an INVITE at 32 seconds is applying Timer B's number to Timer C's job.

fault.title: Proxy gave up at 32 seconds
fault.symptom: A proxy cancels every INVITE at 32 seconds while the downstream phone is still ringing. The operator calls it Timer C.
fault.log:
Proxy log: Timer C expired at 32000 ms, sending CANCEL
Downstream: 180 Ringing still in flight
T1=500ms

Timer C is defined as T1

fault.why: Timer B is 64 times T1 on the transaction. The proxy's INVITE arm is Timer C.
fault.cause: The proxy used the transaction give-up number for the proxy timer.
fault.fix: Set Timer C above 3 minutes unless you have a measured reason and a documented peer requirement. Leave Timer B at 64 times T1.

lessons.title: UDP, TCP, TLS, and WebSocket
lessons.summary: The transport is a property of the hop, written in Via, and it changes retransmission and framing rather than the SIP methods.
objectives: Match UDP, TCP, and TLS to their default ports
Use Content-Length as the stream framing
Read a teaching dial-peer and trusted list

illustration.title: Same SIP, different hop
illustration.caption: A proxy can receive UDP and send TCP. Each Via records the transport that hop actually used.

paragraphs: The transport token and the sent-by value are written after the sender picks how to reach the next hop. The response is sent back toward that Via. If the packet arrives from a different address, the receiver adds a received parameter.

RFC 3581 adds rport so the response can go to the source port the request actually used. That is symmetric response routing. It does not replace a registration or a GRUU when you need to reach the UA later.

sections.h: Framing, TLS, and a small config
paragraphs: On TCP and TLS the parser reads Content-Length bytes of body after the blank line. UDP should carry Content-Length too, so the same parser works. TLS on 5061 protects SIP. It does not by itself encrypt RTP.

A teaching dial-peer uses session protocol sipv2 and a session target. An IP address trusted list names who may present SIP to the box. debug ccsip messages is how you print the SIP that peer sends. WebSocket uses the same messages with WS or WSS.

lab.title: Read the teaching config
lab.prompt: The config is a dial-peer, a trusted source, an empty profile, and one debug command.
steps: Name the command that prints SIP.
lab.config:
voice service voip
 ip address trusted list
  ipv4 192.0.2.40
!
dial-peer voice 10 voip
 destination-pattern +15551212
 session protocol sipv2
 session target ipv4:192.0.2.40
!
voice class sip-profiles 1
!
debug ccsip messages

check.q: Which command prints SIP messages on this box?
check.why: session protocol sipv2 selects SIP. The debug command is what displays the messages.

fault.title: UDP timers on a TCP hop
fault.symptom: A proxy logs Timer A retransmissions for an INVITE whose top Via is TCP, and the peer sees duplicates.
fault.log:
Via: SIP/2.0/TCP 203.0.113.20;branch=z9hG4bKtcp1
Log: Timer A fired, retransmitting INVITE, T1=500ms
choices: Timer A is for unreliable transports. TCP does not start it
TCP requires Timer A by RFC 3261
fault.why: Reliable transports rely on the connection. The SIP layer does not run Timer A.
fault.cause: The transaction code ignored the transport token.
fault.fix: Start Timer A only for unreliable transports. Keep Timer B for both, and use Content-Length on the TCP hop.
